outcome: Nothing since 26 January 2024 has changed whether the Wolstenholme primes are infinite: the known list is still 16843 and 2124679, the search bound is still 10^11 (arXiv:2101.11157 v2, March 2022), and no proof, disproof or changed conjecture appears in any source read; the post-window items are a 2026 proof of the classical mod p^3 Wolstenholme theorem, 2026 characterisations of the primes, and a 2026 AI-credited Lean formalisation of the mod p^3 theorem, none of which bears on infinitude.
problem_asks: One question: is the set of Wolstenholme primes infinite? It asks for no count, no bound on the next term, no characterisation and no density. The object is the set of primes p with C(2p-1, p-1) congruent to 1 mod p^4, equivalently p dividing the numerator of the Bernoulli number B_{p-3} (Wikipedia's current article says p > 7; Reyes-Bustos et al. and Pain use p >= 5; the instances 16843 and 2124679 are unaffected). The frozen statement does not define the object, so this definition is taken from the sources read.

events.what_happened: 16843 is found to be a Wolstenholme prime. The 2007 McIntosh-Roettger introduction, as shown in a search excerpt (their page was not opened), says it was found 'though not explicitly reported' by Selfridge and Pollack in 1964. The PrimePages page for 16843 (opened) gives no discoverer or date.
events.delivers: Exhibits the smallest Wolstenholme prime, p = 16843. One instance of a set whose infinitude is asked; it does not bear on whether further instances exist.
events.remains: The whole question: whether the set is infinite.
events.directly_checkable: Yes: a finite modular check that C(2p-1, p-1) is congruent to 1 mod p^4 at p = 16843. Not rerun here.
events.direction: Adds one instance of the defining congruence; cuts neither way on infinitude.
events.object: The prime 16843, the smallest Wolstenholme prime: a direct instance of the defining congruence, not a family.

events.what_happened: 2124679 is found to be a Wolstenholme prime by Buhler, Crandall, Ernvall and Metsankyla, in 'Irregular primes and cyclotomic invariants to four million', Math. Comp. 61(203), 1993. The reference is as listed on the OEIS A088164 page (opened). The attribution of 2124679 to this paper comes from a search excerpt of the 2007 McIntosh-Roettger paper, whose page could not be opened.
events.delivers: Exhibits the second known Wolstenholme prime, p = 2124679, found during a search for irregular primes. One instance; it does not bear on infinitude.
events.remains: The whole question: whether the set is infinite.

events.what_happened: Richard J. McIntosh, 'On the converse of Wolstenholme's theorem', Acta Arithmetica 71 (1995), as listed in the OEIS A088164 references (opened). Search excerpts, not opened, attribute to this paper the introduction of the name 'Wolstenholme prime', a search reporting no further examples with p < 2 x 10^8, and a conjecture that infinitely many Wolstenholme primes exist.
events.delivers: As reported by search excerpts only: a search to 2 x 10^8 with no new instance, and a conjecture of infinitude. The conjecture restates the question; it is not a result about it.

events.what_happened: R. J. McIntosh and E. L. Roettger, 'A search for Fibonacci-Wieferich and Wolstenholme primes', Math. Comp. 76 (2007), 2087-2094. The abstract, shown in a search excerpt, reports no new Wolstenholme primes p < 10^9. The AMS page returned HTTP 403 and was not opened. The OEIS comment (opened) records the consequence: any further term must exceed 10^9.
events.delivers: A search to 10^9 finds no further instance. This checks finitely many primes and, on the test in section 2.1, does not move the infinitude question. It does set a lower bound of 10^9 on any third Wolstenholme prime.

events.what_happened: Romeo Mestrovic, 'Congruences for Wolstenholme primes', arXiv:1108.4178, first submitted 21 August 2011. The abstract states that for a Wolstenholme prime C(2p-1, p-1) is congruent to 1 - 2p*Sum(1/k) - 2p^2*Sum(1/k^2) mod p^7 (sums over k = 1..p-1), and that this congruence forces p to be a Wolstenholme prime. The OEIS reference list gives the journal version as Czechoslovak Math. J. 65 (2015); not opened.
events.revisions: Journal version Czechoslovak Math. J. 65 (2015), per the OEIS reference list (not opened).
events.delivers: Characterises Wolstenholme primes by a mod p^7 congruence, in both directions per the abstract. Restates the set; does not count or bound it.
events.remains: The whole question: whether the characterised set is infinite.
events.direction: A characterisation; cuts neither way on infinitude.

events.what_happened: Romeo Mestrovic, 'Variations of Lucas' Theorem Modulo Prime Powers', arXiv:1301.0252, first submitted 29 December 2012. The abstract gives a simple inductive proof of a Davis-Webb variation of Lucas's theorem for primes p >= 5 and states that it yields 'a new characterization of Wolstenholme primes'.
events.delivers: A new characterisation of Wolstenholme primes, per the author's abstract. Restates the set; does not count or bound it.
events.doubts: The 'new characterization' is the author's own claim; the body was not read.
events.direction: A characterisation; cuts neither way on infinitude.

events.what_happened: Christian Aebi and Grant Cairns, 'Wolstenholme again', arXiv:1502.05750, first submitted 19 February 2015. The abstract gives an elementary, self-contained proof of the equivalence of a collection of Wolstenholme-type congruences due to Helou and Terjanian. A search excerpt also attributes to this paper an equivalence with harmonic sums and a mod p^5 statement; neither appears in the abstract, and I did not read the body.
events.delivers: An equivalence among Wolstenholme-type congruences, which characterises the primes in the family the abstract names. The specific congruences are not stated in the abstract. Restates the set; does not count or bound it.
events.doubts: The harmonic-sum and mod p^5 claims come from a search excerpt and are not confirmed here.
events.direction: An equivalence of congruences; cuts neither way on infinitude.

events.what_happened: Andrew R. Booker, Shehzad Hathi, Michael J. Mossinghoff and Timothy S. Trudgian, 'Wolstenholme and Vandiver primes', arXiv:2101.11157. Version 1, first submitted 27 January 2021 (the listing shows 26 January), states that 'no additional Wolstenholme primes exist up to 60 billion' (search extended by a factor of 6) and 'no additional Vandiver primes occur up to 40 billion'. Version 2, revised 27 March 2022, states 10^11 for both. Theorem 1.1 of v2 lists the Wolstenholme primes below 10^11 as 16843 and 2124679. The paper is cited as published in The Ramanujan Journal (Wikipedia citation, opened).
events.revisions: v1 27 Jan 2021 (search to 6 x 10^10); v2 27 Mar 2022 (search to 10^11, Vandiver to 10^11 as well). No v3 listed.
events.delivers: A computational result: no Wolstenholme prime p with 2124679 < p < 10^11 (v2; v1 claimed this only up to 6 x 10^10). It gives a lower bound on any third Wolstenholme prime. It checks finitely many primes and so, on the test in section 2.1, does not move the infinitude question; it does move the known bound on the next term.
events.remains: Whether there are infinitely many Wolstenholme primes; whether there is a third one at all.

events.what_happened: Leonardo Carofiglio, Luigi De Filpo and Alessandro Gambini, 'p-adic valuation of harmonic sums and their connections with Wolstenholme primes', arXiv:2303.15010, first submitted 27 March 2023, journal reference Indian Journal of Pure and Applied Mathematics (2023), as stated on the arXiv page. They study an Eswarathasan-Levine conjecture on p-adic valuations of harmonic numbers and prove two results on v_p(H(p^m n)) when v_p(H(n)) = 3, one for Wolstenholme primes (Theorem 2.6) and one for non-Wolstenholme primes (Theorem 2.5).
events.delivers: Results about the p-adic valuation of harmonic numbers along multiples of p, split by whether p is a Wolstenholme prime. They do not give a criterion for Wolstenholme primes, a search bound, or a statement about how many there are. The abstract does not say that they settle the Eswarathasan-Levine conjecture.
events.remains: The whole question: whether the set of Wolstenholme primes is infinite.

events.what_happened: Cid Reyes-Bustos, Naoya Yamaguchi and Yuka Yamaguchi, 'Wolstenholme primes and group determinants of cyclic groups', arXiv:2311.00010, first submitted 31 October 2023. Theorem 2.2 gives an equivalent definition: p is a Wolstenholme prime if and only if N(Theta(C_p)) is congruent to 1 mod p^3, where N counts the terms of the group determinant of the cyclic group C_p. The paper states that it is conjectured that the set of Wolstenholme primes is infinite, based on arguments using the prime number theorem. Published in Proc. Japan Acad. Ser. A 100(9) (2024), per a search result; the journal page was not opened.

events.what_happened: Nikita Kalinin, 'Wolstenholme's theorem over Gaussian integers', arXiv:2504.07978, submitted 30 March 2025. For primes p > 7 it proves that the sum of inverses of Gaussian integers satisfies S_p = 0 mod p^4, extends this to higher-power sums, proposes conjectures, and tabulates p <= 1000.
events.delivers: A result over the Gaussian integers Z[i], an analogue of Wolstenholme's theorem. It says nothing about Wolstenholme primes in the integers.
events.remains: The whole question for the integers, which this paper does not touch.
events.direction: An analogue over a different ring; discounted for this problem.

It proves a polynomial congruence mod p for pairs with sqrt(d), extending a conjecture of N. Kalinin, and a Wolstenholme-type congruence mod p^2 for a sum of 1/(m + n sqrt(d)).

It generalises partial Lucas congruences that Chamberland and Dilcher found for a binomial sum related to Wolstenholme's theorem, to a general class of constant-term sequences.

events.what_happened: Jean-Christophe Pain, 'A proof of Wolstenholme's theorem and congruence properties via an Egorychev-type integral', arXiv:2604.03000, submitted 3 April 2026 (single version). It proves the classical mod p^3 Wolstenholme theorem by a contour integral. Section 8.1 (opened HTML) defines Wolstenholme primes as primes dividing the numerator of B_{p-3} and says the computation 'confirms Glaisher's refinement': for Wolstenholme primes C(2p-1, p-1) is congruent to 1 mod p^4 exactly.
events.delivers: A new proof of the mod p^3 theorem and a re-derivation of the mod p^4 refinement that Glaisher had already given, per the paper's own attribution. It does not find a new Wolstenholme prime and says nothing about how many there are.
events.time_since_posted: About 6 months to 11 October 2026; no later engagement found in the searches run.
events.directly_checkable: The argument is a written proof; the classical theorem can be checked by hand.
events.direction: Re-proves known results about Wolstenholme's theorem and the mod p^4 characterisation; cuts neither way on infinitude.

events.what_happened: Evan Chen, Chris Cummins, Ben Eltschig, Dejan Grubisic, Leopold Haller, Letong Hong, Andranik Kurghinyan, Kenny Lau, Hugh Leather, Seewoo Lee, Aram Markosyan, Ken Ono, Manooshree Patel, Gaurang Pendharkar, Vedant Rathi, Alex Schneidman, Volker Seeker, Shubho Sengupta, Ishan Sinha, Jimmy Xin, Jujian Zhang, 'Almost all primes are partially regular', arXiv:2602.05090, submitted 4 February 2026. For a density-one set of odd primes p, the eigenspaces of the p-part of the class group of Q(zeta_p) vanish for characters omega^(p-2k) with 2 <= 2k <= sqrt(p)/(log p)^alpha, alpha > 1/2 (equivalently p does not divide the numerator of B_(2k) in that range). Consequences include a partial Vandiver theorem. The authors state the theorem is fully formalised in Lean/Mathlib (Lean 4.26.0) and was produced automatically by AxiomProver.
events.delivers: A density-one statement about Bernoulli numerators B_(2k) for indices up to sqrt(p)/(log p)^alpha, with a partial Vandiver theorem as a consequence. The paper does not mention Wolstenholme primes. The Wolstenholme condition involves B_(p-3), an index near p, which is outside the stated range; I read that as not reaching the Wolstenholme condition, and the judging pass should weigh it.
events.remains: Whole problem: nothing in the stated range bears on whether p divides B_(p-3) for infinitely many p. Full Vandiver's conjecture remains open per the paper.
events.time_since_posted: About 8 months to 11 October 2026; the searches found only AI-generated summary pages and the company blog, and I did not read the arXiv comments field.

events.what_happened: Alexandre Linhares, 'Deep Vision: A Formal Proof of Wolstenholme's Theorem in Lean 4', arXiv:2604.16507, first submitted 14 April 2026, revised 9 August 2026. It gives a Lean 4 (Mathlib) formal verification of the mod p^3 theorem (C(2p-1, p-1) congruent to 1 mod p^3 for primes p >= 5), with zero sorry declarations, and states this is the first formal verification of that theorem in Lean 4 to the author's knowledge. The abstract says the proof 'was discovered through a collaboration between a relational analogy engine for theorem proving' and human-directed formalisation. Sections 3.3 and 4 credit the tactic search to 'Deep Vision' and the final proofs to an LLM, Claude. The paper calls the theorem 'closely related to Wolstenholme primes' and states no result about the mod p^4 condition or about infinitude.
events.revisions: v1 14 Apr 2026; v2 9 Aug 2026. The two fetched readings disagree on the author line and the AI disclosure: the v1 reading says 'Claude Code' appears as an author-line entry and that there is no formal AI disclosure; the v2 reading says 'Neither tool is listed as an author' and quotes a disclosure. Check against the PDF.
events.delivers: A formal (Lean 4) proof of the mod p^3 Wolstenholme theorem only. It does not establish the mod p^4 characterisation, count Wolstenholme primes, or bear on infinitude. Wolstenholme's theorem is the weaker congruence in the Wolstenholme-prime definition; the paper states no result for the stronger one.
events.remains: The whole question: the paper states nothing about the mod p^4 condition or about infinitude.

The abstract says they 'establish a criterion involving Wolstenholme primes' for congruence properties of the number of monomials in group permanents. Corollary 1.8 gives the cyclic-group analogue mod p^3.

disputes.summary: The search bound for Wolstenholme primes is stated differently across versions and sources: v1 of arXiv:2101.11157 says 'no additional Wolstenholme primes exist up to 60 billion'; v2 (27 March 2022) says 10^11; Wikipedia says 10^11; an OEIS comment (21 April 2021) says a third term would exceed 6 x 10^10; McIntosh and Roettger (2007) reported 10^9; older Wikipedia mirrors in search excerpts give 10^9. The record uses 10^11 as the current figure and keeps 60 billion as the v1 history.

The infinitude conjecture is attributed to McIntosh (1995) in search excerpts. Wikipedia (opened) and Reyes-Bustos et al. (opened) say only that it is conjectured, and no opened source states where it first appeared. Wikipedia's 'roughly one between 10^11 and 10^24' appears in search excerpts and not in the fetched text.

The two fetched readings of arXiv:2604.16507 disagree on the author line ('Claude Code' appears as an author-line entry in the v1 reading; 'Neither tool is listed as an author' in the v2 reading) and on the AI disclosure (no formal disclosure in the v1 reading; a disclosure quoted in the v2 reading). This must be checked against the PDF before the AI attribution is relied on.

summary: Nothing bearing on whether Wolstenholme primes are infinite has happened since 26 January 2024. The Wikipedia article (last edited 21 August 2026 per its footer, opened) still gives the known primes 16843 and 2124679, a search bound of 10^11 'as of 2022', and the question as open, and the Booker-Hathi-Mossinghoff-Trudgian search (arXiv:2101.11157 v2, opened) is still the latest computation I found. Pre-window events set out the instances and bounds: discoveries of 16843 (1964, unreported) and 2124679 (1993), McIntosh's 1995 converse paper (abstract not read) and the McIntosh-Roettger search to 10^9 (2007; AMS page refused, abstract via excerpt), characterisations by Mestrovic (2011, 2012), Aebi-Cairns (2015), Carofiglio et al. (2023) and Reyes-Bustos et al. (2023), and the 2021 search to 10^11. Post-window items: Pain (arXiv:2604.03000, 3 April 2026, opened) reproves the mod p^3 theorem and the mod p^4 refinement that Glaisher had already given, with no new instance; Yamaguchi and Yamaguchi (arXiv:2606.23765, 22 June 2026, opened) prove characterisations by group permanents; Kalinin (2025), Jiang and Sun (2025), Straub (2025), Calderon (2026) and Zeng (2026) are analogues or q-analogues that do not mention the prime question. The AI picture: two AI-credited items sit near this problem and neither is about the prime question. Linhares (arXiv:2604.16507, 14 April 2026, revised 9 August 2026) gives a Lean 4 formal proof of the mod p^3 Wolstenholme theorem and credits its discovery to 'Deep Vision', the author's 'relational analogy engine', with Claude as the LLM that writes the final proofs; the paper says the theorem is 'closely related to Wolstenholme primes' and states no result about them. AxiomProver (arXiv:2602.05090, 4 February 2026, opened) autonomously produced a Lean-verified proof of a density-one partial-regularity theorem for Bernoulli numerators in a small-index range; it does not mention Wolstenholme primes. Where a call is close: the Linhares item is an AI contribution in the Wolstenholme area, but its mathematics is the classical mod p^3 theorem and the authors' own description of the engine is the only evidence for the AI role. The AxiomProver statement is nearest the defining Bernoulli condition, but its stated range 2k <= sqrt(p)/(log p)^alpha does not reach index p-3, the index in the Wolstenholme condition; that reading is mine, and the paper does not discuss Wolstenholme primes. Searches: 49 web searches including about a dozen AI-targeted ones (OpenAI, DeepMind, AlphaEvolve, Claude/Anthropic, Lean, Aristotle, AxiomProver, Erdos); none surfaced the Linhares paper or any AI-credited Wolstenholme-prime result, and it was found only through the arXiv listing. The OpenAI 722-manuscript catalogue (Oct 2026) and the Astra list (Aug 2026) show no Wolstenholme entry in what I could read, but I could not read the whole catalogue (see incomplete). No withdrawal, retraction or published critique was found for any event.
competing_reading: Read the 2021-22 search as moving a quantity the question names: the expected count of Wolstenholme primes between K and N (roughly ln ln N - ln ln K, per Wikipedia and the heuristic in Reyes-Bustos et al.) and the 'known' list both depend on the search bound, so the extension to 10^11 updates a quantity the problem is about. On the section 2.1 test it checks finitely many primes and settles nothing about infinitude. For the Linhares paper, one could argue it is a real AI contribution to the Wolstenholme area because it is 'closely related to Wolstenholme primes' and Wolstenholme's theorem is the weaker half of the defining congruence; against that, it states no result about the primes, and its AI role rests on the author's own accounts whose v1 and v2 readings disagree.
what_would_settle_it: For infinitude: a proof that infinitely many p satisfy C(2p-1, p-1) congruent to 1 mod p^4, a proof that only finitely many do, or a proof that p does not divide B_(p-3) for infinitely many p (a related open conjecture). A third Wolstenholme prime would change the known list but would not settle infinitude. For the AI question on arXiv:2604.16507: the PDF's author line and AI disclosure, the Lean repository, and the ARGO LABS report that Yanasse cites (arXiv:2604.17229) for how Deep Vision works. For AxiomProver: the Lean repository, its sorry status, and any statement by the authors on whether the Bernoulli range bears on B_(p-3).

events.ai_basis: The theorem proving partial regularity for almost all p is fully formalized in Lean/Mathlib and was produced automatically by AxiomProver from a natural-language statement of the conjecture.

events.credibility_reason: Author's own accounts of the AI role and line counts differ between v1 and v2; no independent engagement.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether the set is infinite. Discoveries of 16843 and 2124679 and the searches to 10^9 and 10^11 are finite checks of a universal question, so they are instances; a lower bound on a third prime is not a quantity the statement asks about. Characterisations (Mestrovic, Aebi-Cairns, Reyes-Bustos et al., Yamaguchi-Yamaguchi) restate the set and bound nothing: none. Analogues over Z[i], Z[sqrt d], q-analogues and harmonic-valuation results are variants. Pain re-proves known theorems: none. AxiomProver's theorem concerns Bernoulli numerators at small indices, not B_(p-3), so it is a variant; its own quote supports generated, which the harness discards with the scope. Linhares formalises the classical mod p^3 theorem (1862), a formalisation of a known result, so scope none and AI role none under the rule that formalising an already-proved argument is not mathematics in the result.
judgement.doubts: Linhares AI role: one could argue Deep Vision/Claude produced a new proof rather than formalising an existing one; it is irrelevant here since the event bears on the mod p^3 theorem, not on infinitude. Pre-1995/2007 attributions rest partly on search excerpts.
